VIDEO.title: Christians Have Made the Gospel Too Small
VIDEO.series: The Book of Romans, Every Word (playlist of 28 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Romans 15:14-33 · Episode 27 (#27 of 28 in the playlist)
SUMMARY: The teacher opens: near the end of Romans it feels like Paul is winding down, with travel plans and an offering for Jerusalem. But tucked inside those details is strange language that, traced back through the Old Testament, shows Paul doing something much bigger. He reads Romans 15:14-33: Paul is convinced the Romans are full of goodness and knowledge (15:14); he has written boldly as a minister of Christ to the Gentiles, ministering the gospel as a priest (15:15-16); he boasts only in what Christ has done through him, from Jerusalem to Illyricum (15:17-19); his ambition is to preach where Christ is not named (15:20-21); Jerusalem, then Rome, then Spain (15:22-29); a request for prayer and a blessing (15:30-33).

Observations: after confronting sin and hypocrisy (Romans 2, 6, 11), Paul affirms the church (15:14). They were not uninformed, but still vulnerable to misapplication and blind spots. Paul describes his ministry in priestly terms, with the Gentiles as his offering, sanctified by the Spirit: his goal is not just conversion but a holy people. He boasts only in Christ. He pushes the gospel into unreached places, trusting established churches to be strengthened by teaching and letters.

Places and timeline: Paul planted churches in Macedonia and Achaia (Acts 16-18): Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Corinth. He most likely wrote Romans around Acts 20:1-3, probably from Corinth. Former pagans were funding Jewish believers in Jerusalem, Romans 11 in action. His Jerusalem trip comes in Acts 21, which explains his request for prayer (15:30-31). The God of peace (15:33): peace is something God gives.

Old Testament background: the nations brought as an offering, with some taken as priests and Levites (Isaiah 66:19-21); Spirit-empowered cleansing and a new heart (Ezekiel 36:25-27); signs and wonders as in the exodus (Deuteronomy 4:34), now a new exodus for the nations; the law going forth from Zion (Isaiah 2:2-3; compare Acts 1:8); the Servant who sprinkles many nations (Isaiah 52:15, quoted in 15:21).

Paul pulls from all of the Tanakh, Law, Prophets and Writings, to show that Gentile inclusion was always God's plan: not a backup plan triggered by Israel's failure, but the fulfillment of His promises. God didn't just save sinners from something; He saved them for something.
The lesson: 'The gospel doesn't merely rescue sinners. … It actually transforms them into a consecrated people who participate in God's work of reconciling the nations and strengthening his people.'
QUOTES: The gospel doesn't merely rescue sinners. It certainly rescues them, but it doesn't merely do that. It actually transforms them into a consecrated people who participate in God's work of reconciling the nations and strengthening his people.
God didn't just save sinners from something. He saved them for something.
The question for us today is not merely whether we've received the gospel... It's actually whether our lives now reflect the gospel's priestly calling.
We mistake our preferences for holiness. Our instincts for wisdom. We mistake our tribes for faithfulness and our self-expression for freedom.

method.p: In Romans 15:14-33 circle every place name (Jerusalem, Illyricum, Spain, Macedonia, Achaia, Judea, Rome) and underline the priestly words (minister, ministering as a priest, offering, acceptable, sanctified). Then read Isaiah 66:19-21 and mark the same ideas.

BACKGROUND.p: Paul organized this gift over several years: 'Now concerning the collection for the saints' (1 Corinthians 16:1); see also 2 Corinthians 8-9 and Galatians 2:10. Later he told Felix he had come 'to bring alms to my nation' (Acts 24:17).

Illyricum was a Roman province on the eastern Adriatic. Spain, at the western end of the Mediterranean, had been Roman for centuries and was thoroughly Latin-speaking. Rome would be the natural base for a western mission.

Paul's words in 15:16, minister, ministering as a priest, offering, acceptable, sanctified, are temple vocabulary. Israel itself was called 'a kingdom of priests' (Exodus 19:6); Peter calls the church 'a royal priesthood' (1 Peter 2:9).

DEBATES.p: Acts ends with Paul in Rome, so the New Testament does not say. Clement of Rome, writing about AD 96, says Paul reached the limits of the West, which some take to mean Spain; others think his plans were cut short.

Some scholars suggest Paul read Isaiah 66:19-20, with its list of distant nations, as a map for the Gentile mission, a reading close to the video's. Others think Isaiah shaped his theology of the offering more than his itinerary.

DEBATES.h: What was the collection meant to do?
DEBATES.p: Relief for the poor (15:26), a sign of unity between Gentile and Jewish believers (15:27, as the video stresses), or both, perhaps also the nations' gifts flowing to Zion.

CAREFUL: The outline says Paul explains his strategy of preaching where Christ is not named 'in verses 28 to 29'; that strategy is 15:20-21, and the travel plans are 15:22-29. The captions may have garbled 'verses 20 to 29.'

The video reads Romans 11 as 'Do not be arrogant toward the branches'; the LSB has 'do not boast against the branches' (11:18) and 'Do not be haughty, but fear' (11:20). Same verses, different translation.

QUESTIONS: What is the difference between being saved from something and being saved for something?
How does seeing the Gentiles as Paul's 'offering' change how you see evangelism?
Why would Gentile churches owe material help to Jerusalem (15:27)?
Where do you mistake preferences for holiness, or tribes for faithfulness?
Does your life reflect the gospel's priestly calling toward others this week?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: If Paul graded us on unity, honor and obedience to God's purpose, the teacher doubts we would pass, and he says that starts with him. A talk he gave in Boston on the disappearance of truth made him see how the church has absorbed worldly values. One great failure of the modern church, especially in America, is unconsciously absorbing expressive individualism while still speaking the language of Christian community. We call the church a covenant family but approach it as consumers. When conflict comes over disputable matters such as culture, worship styles, schooling, alcohol or entertainment, we respond not with patience and mutual edification but by leaving, dividing and self-sorting into tribes, turning secondary matters into markers of righteousness. In the spirit of Christ's lament (Matthew 23:37), he cries out for a modern church rescued by the same mercy and sent on the same mission, yet divided: 'Jesus Christ calls us to one table, but we keep building walls around it.' He closes in prayer for forgiveness, consecration and unity, that the church would be marked by truth and steadfast love, where righteousness and peace kiss (Psalm 85:10).
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): pick one practical, material way to serve believers outside your own circle this month, perhaps a church of a different background, as Macedonia and Achaia did for Jerusalem.

## Jerusalem, Rome and Spain
1. Romans 15:25-27: The collection for Jerusalem
   Romans 11 in action Romans 15:26-27: "For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to share with the poor among the saints in Jerusalem. Yes, they were pleased to do so, and they are indebted to them. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they are indebted to minister to them also in material things." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Romans+15:26-27
   (video) Paul planted churches in Macedonia and Achaia (Acts 16-18): Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Corinth, urban trade hubs. Former pagans now funding Jewish believers in Jerusalem are a real-world example of the unity Paul calls for in Romans 14-15: Gentiles grafted in and showing gratitude to Israel.
2. Romans 15:22-24, 28-29; Acts 20:2-3: Jerusalem, Rome, Spain
   Luke (Acts 20:2-3, LSB): "And when he had gone through those districts and had given them much exhortation, he came to Greece. And there he spent three months, and when a plot was formed against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia."
   Paul (Romans 15:28, LSB): "Therefore, when I have completed this and have put my seal on this fruit of theirs, I will go on by way of you to Spain."
   (video) Paul most likely wrote Romans around Acts 20:1-3, probably in Corinth or Achaia. His trip to Jerusalem comes after the letter, in Acts 21.
3. Romans 15:30-33: Strive together in prayer
   The God of peace Romans 15:30-31: "Now I urge you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God for me, that I may be rescued from those who are disobedient in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may prove acceptable to the saints;" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Romans+15:30-31
   (video) If you know Acts, you see where this is headed (Acts 21). 'Now may the God of peace be with you all. Amen' (Romans 15:33): after division, mission and tension, peace is not assumed; God gives it. (Romans 15:33)

## Key people
- Isaiah: The nations as an offering (66:19-21), Zion's law going forth (2:2-3), the Servant who sprinkles many nations (52:15). [Background] Prophet in Jerusalem (Isaiah 1:1).
- Ezekiel: A new heart and God's Spirit within (36:25-27). [Background] Priest and prophet among the exiles in Babylon (Ezekiel 1:1-3).
- Moses: Signs and wonders in the exodus (Deuteronomy 4:34). [Background] Lawgiver of Israel (Deuteronomy 34:10).
- The saints in Jerusalem: The poor among them receive the Gentile churches' contribution (15:26). [Background] Paul had agreed to 'remember the poor' (Galatians 2:10).

## Places [Background]
- Jerusalem (named in the video): Starting point of Paul's mission and destination of the collection (15:19, 25).
- Illyricum (Salona) (named in the video): The northwestern edge of Paul's preaching so far (15:19).
- Philippi (named in the video): A church in Macedonia that gave to the collection (Acts 16).
- Thessalonica (named in the video): Macedonian church (Acts 17).
- Berea (named in the video): Macedonian church (Acts 17).
- Corinth (named in the video): Chief city of Achaia, where Paul probably wrote Romans (Acts 20:2-3).
- Rome (named in the video): Paul's stop on the way to Spain (15:24, 28).

## Key terms
- Priestly service: Paul's description of his gospel ministry, with the Gentiles as his offering (15:16).
- Sanctified: Made holy, set apart for God; here by the Holy Spirit (15:16).
- Illyricum: Roman province along the Adriatic; the northwestern edge of Paul's mission (15:19).
- The collection: Money gathered by Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem (15:25-27).
- Tanakh: The Hebrew Bible: Law, Prophets and Writings.
- Expressive individualism: The video's term for absorbing the culture's focus on self-expression while speaking the language of Christian community.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- The collection for Jerusalem: Paul organized this gift over several years: 'Now concerning the collection for the saints' (1 Corinthians 16:1); see also 2 Corinthians 8-9 and Galatians 2:10. Later he told Felix he had come 'to bring alms to my nation' (Acts 24:17).
- Illyricum and Spain: Illyricum was a Roman province on the eastern Adriatic. Spain, at the western end of the Mediterranean, had been Roman for centuries and was thoroughly Latin-speaking. Rome would be the natural base for a western mission.
- Priestly language: Paul's words in 15:16, minister, ministering as a priest, offering, acceptable, sanctified, are temple vocabulary. Israel itself was called 'a kingdom of priests' (Exodus 19:6); Peter calls the church 'a royal priesthood' (1 Peter 2:9).

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "Observe the lowly-mindedness of Paul, observe his wisdom, how he gave a deep cut in the former part, and then when he had succeeded in what he wished, how he uses much kindliness next." Homilies on Romans 29, on 15:14-15. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "For to me this is a priesthood, this preaching and declaring. This is the sacrifice I bring." Homilies on Romans 29, on 15:16. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "So far was he from thrusting himself upon other men's disciples, and from doing this for glory's sake, that he even made it a point to teach those who had not heard." Homilies on Romans 29, on 15:20. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Did Paul reach Spain? Acts ends with Paul in Rome, so the New Testament does not say. Clement of Rome, writing about AD 96, says Paul reached the limits of the West, which some take to mean Spain; others think his plans were cut short.
- Did Isaiah 66 shape Paul's route? Some scholars suggest Paul read Isaiah 66:19-20, with its list of distant nations, as a map for the Gentile mission, a reading close to the video's. Others think Isaiah shaped his theology of the offering more than his itinerary.
- What was the collection meant to do? Relief for the poor (15:26), a sign of unity between Gentile and Jewish believers (15:27, as the video stresses), or both, perhaps also the nations' gifts flowing to Zion.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The outline says Paul explains his strategy of preaching where Christ is not named 'in verses 28 to 29'; that strategy is 15:20-21, and the travel plans are 15:22-29. The captions may have garbled 'verses 20 to 29.'
- The video reads Romans 11 as 'Do not be arrogant toward the branches'; the LSB has 'do not boast against the branches' (11:18) and 'Do not be haughty, but fear' (11:20). Same verses, different translation.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. What is the difference between being saved from something and being saved for something?
2. How does seeing the Gentiles as Paul's 'offering' change how you see evangelism?
3. Why would Gentile churches owe material help to Jerusalem (15:27)?
4. Where do you mistake preferences for holiness, or tribes for faithfulness?
5. Does your life reflect the gospel's priestly calling toward others this week?

## Application
- (video) If Paul graded us on unity, honor and obedience to God's purpose, the teacher doubts we would pass, and he says that starts with him. A talk he gave in Boston on the disappearance of truth made him see how the church has absorbed worldly values. One great failure of the modern church, especially in America, is unconsciously absorbing expressive individualism while still speaking the language of Christian community. We call the church a covenant family but approach it as consumers. When conflict comes over disputable matters such as culture, worship styles, schooling, alcohol or entertainment, we respond not with patience and mutual edification but by leaving, dividing and self-sorting into tribes, turning secondary matters into markers of righteousness. In the spirit of Christ's lament (Matthew 23:37), he cries out for a modern church rescued by the same mercy and sent on the same mission, yet divided: 'Jesus Christ calls us to one table, but we keep building walls around it.' He closes in prayer for forgiveness, consecration and unity, that the church would be marked by truth and steadfast love, where righteousness and peace kiss (Psalm 85:10).
- Study note (added): pick one practical, material way to serve believers outside your own circle this month, perhaps a church of a different background, as Macedonia and Achaia did for Jerusalem.
